meetings.title: Maya / Raj 1:1
segments: Hey Raj. How are you doing, honestly?
It's been a heavy couple of weeks.
Honestly, tired. The outage took a lot out of the team, and out of me.
But the postmortem went better than I expected.
People were really constructive about it.
How are Sam and Lena doing?
They carried a lot of that night.
Sam was shaken. It was his first real incident as incident commander, and he was hard on himself afterwards.
I told him he handled it well, which he did.
Lena's fine, she's seen worse at her last job.
She actually enjoyed digging into the lock.
It might be worth telling Sam in front of the team what he did well.
It lands differently when it's public.
Good idea. I'll do it at the next team retro.
I thought the postmortem was excellent.
Clear, no blame, and the follow-ups were specific.
Chris mentioned it to me unprompted, which he doesn't usually do.
Honestly, a lot of the credit goes to Lena.
She wrote most of the timeline section, and it's the clearest part of the document.
That's good to hear. Thank you.
What's on your mind for this week?
Two things. First, on-call. With five engineers, everyone is on call every fifth week, and after the outage, people are nervous about it.
Sam hasn't really slept properly on his last two shifts.
I don't think that's sustainable.
What would make it sustainable?
Either more people in the rotation, or fewer pages.
We're working on fewer pages, the queue lag alert helped.
But realistically we need the staff data engineer hire, and maybe share the rotation with the growth team.
How many pages did on-call get last week, roughly?
Eleven. Before the outage it was more like three or four a week.
Some of that is the new alerts being a bit too sensitive, which we'll tune.
But some of it is real, the ingest system is under more load than it was designed for.
Is there a quick win to reduce the noise while the hire happens?
Yes, tuning the lag alert thresholds.
Sam's already on it. That should get us back to five or six a week.
Okay. I'll talk to Chris about accelerating the staff data engineer role, and I'll ask the growth team lead about a shared rotation.
I can't promise the second one, but I'll push.
Thanks. The second thing is the alignment meeting.
I'm worried I'm going to walk in and be asked to do SSO and Jira and Insights all at once.
We can't. I'd rather say that clearly than nod and then miss.
What if someone pushes back in the room?
Aisha will want SSO yesterday.
Then I'll show what we'd have to drop to do it faster.
If the answer is 'pause the outage hardening', I'll say no, and I'd want you to back me.
If it's 'drop Jira', that's a business call, and I'm happy for the group to make it.
That's exactly the right framing.
Reliability isn't on the table, scope is.
I want you to say exactly that.
Can you bring actual numbers?
People, weeks, what's already committed.
It's much easier for everyone to make a trade-off when the math is on the screen.
One thing I want to check with you before I build it.
Should I include the outage hardening as committed work, or present it as something we could pause?
Committed. We are not pausing reliability work to make a roadmap look better.
If someone asks, I'll back you on that in the room.
Thank you. That makes the conversation a lot easier.
Yes. I'll put together a capacity breakdown before the alignment meeting.
Can I also ask for some feedback?
Anything I could be doing differently for you or the team?
Honestly, one thing. Sometimes priorities change after a conversation between you and sales that I'm not part of.
By the time it reaches me, it's already decided.
I'd rather be in the room earlier, even just to say 'that's three weeks, not one.'
That's fair, and thank you for saying it.
I'll add you to the weekly roadmap sync with Aisha.
If that ends up being too much of your time, tell me.
Should I bring anything to the first roadmap sync?
Just your current capacity picture.
Aisha will bring the deals that need engineering input.
The goal is that no commitment goes to a customer without you seeing it first.
That would really help.
Last thing, growth. Last time you mentioned wanting to move toward engineering management.
Is that still where your head is?
Yes. I like the technical work, but the part I've enjoyed most this year is helping Sam and Lena grow.
I'd like to be managing the platform team formally within a year.
What does managing formally mean to you?
What would change day to day?
Less coding, for sure. More time on hiring, career conversations, and making sure the team has what they need.
Honestly, I already do half of that.
It would just be official, and I'd stop feeling guilty about not writing code.
The guilt is real. Most new managers feel it.
I think that's very realistic.
Two concrete things. Lead the hiring loop for the staff data engineer, end to end.
And let Lena lead the day to day on SAML, with you as the reviewer, rather than doing it yourself.
That's the muscle you'll need.
Letting go of the SAML work will be hard.
But yes, that makes sense.
Good. Let's check in on all of this in two weeks.
Before we go, can I ask how the board feels about the roadmap?
I hear bits and pieces.
Mostly positive. They want to see enterprise traction, which is why SSO keeps coming up.
And they like the Insights story, as long as it's real and not just an AI label.
I'll share more after the board meeting.
Thanks. See you tomorrow.
